Quartic Keller Maps and Tameness in Three Variables

Jie Wang Address: Jie Wang, State Key Laboratory of Mathematical Sciences, Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China Email address: wangjie212@amss.ac.cn and Dan Yan Address: Dan Yan, MOE-LCSM, School of Mathematics and Statistics, Hunan Normal University, Changsha, China Email address: yan-dan-hi@163.com
Date: October 27, 2026
Abstract.

We study invertibility and tameness for polynomial maps of affine three-space of total degree at most four. We prove that every complex Keller map in this degree range is a polynomial automorphism and, independently, that every complex polynomial automorphism of total degree at most four is tame. The invertibility argument combines homogeneous factorization of the leading part, invariant rings of conic pencils, and residue obstructions on cubic fibers. The tameness argument uses a criterion based on a constant second directional derivative, low-degree coordinate classifications, and local tameness of plane polynomial automorphisms over a polynomial parameter ring. The invertibility conclusion extends to every field of characteristic zero.

Key words and phrases: 
Jacobian conjecture; Keller map; polynomial automorphism; tame automorphism; quasi-translation; polynomial invariant ring
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 14R15, 14R10; Secondary 13N15, 14R20

1. Introduction

Polynomial maps with constant nonzero Jacobian determinant connect local algebraic properties with global questions about affine space. The chain rule shows that every polynomial automorphism has constant nonzero Jacobian determinant. The converse is the assertion traditionally known as the Jacobian conjecture, originating in Keller’s work [Kel39]. Its study has led to methods involving formal inverses, homogeneous reductions, polynomial derivations, and the geometry of fibers; see the survey of Bass, Connell, and Wright [BCW82] and the monographs [E00, EKC21].

The general conjecture was disproved in dimension three by the counterexample announced by Levent Alpöge on 19 July 2026 [Alp26]. His map has component total degrees (7,6,4)(7,6,4) and constant Jacobian determinant −2-2, yet identifies three distinct points. Its ordinary total degree is therefore seven, while its geometric degree is three; see [Gao26, Section 3.4]. Tao [Tao26] gives a geometric explanation of the example, and Gao [Gao26] develops the tangent-sweep construction and higher-dimensional extensions. Van den Essen [E26] gives an elementary construction recovering Alpöge’s example up to linear coordinate changes. These examples demonstrate the role of behavior at infinity: a constant nonzero Jacobian determinant gives local invertibility, but does not ensure properness or global injectivity. They also motivate identifying degree ranges and structural hypotheses under which polynomial invertibility still follows.

Degree bounds provide a natural setting in which to study this question. Quadratic Keller maps are invertible in every dimension [Wang80], and Vistoli [Vis99] gave a conceptual proof of invertibility in dimension three and degree three. The previously established results discussed here leave open the invertibility of arbitrary Keller maps in dimension three of ordinary total degrees four, five, and six. In dimension two, Moh [Moh83] established invertibility through degree one hundred; Guccione, Guccione, Horruitiner, and Valqui [GGHV22] subsequently raised the lower bound for a possible counterexample to one hundred and eight. The homogeneous cubic reduction of Bass, Connell, and Wright [BCW82] concerns maps in varying dimension. It therefore does not replace the analysis of arbitrary maps of a fixed degree in three variables. Recent work of de Bondt [dB26] makes this distinction concrete: by economical stabilization of Alpöge’s example, he constructs a cubic Keller counterexample in dimension twelve and a cubic-linear counterexample in dimension ninety, as well as counterexamples to forms of Zhao’s vanishing conjecture. These constructions make the increase in dimension explicit when a high-degree map is replaced by a low-degree one; degree bounds in a fixed dimension require separate arguments.

Recent algebraic work on the planar conjecture gives further constraints on possible counterexamples. Lee and Li [LL24] develop generalized Magnus expansions and restrict the northeastern vertices of the Newton polygons of the associated inner polynomials. Valqui and Ramírez [VR25] compute a Gröbner basis and determine the solution set of a polynomial system arising in a Laurent-series formulation of the planar problem. These works illustrate how expansions and elimination constrain Jacobian pairs; our homogeneous coefficient analysis applies related algebraic tools to quartic leading parts.

The geometry of fibers and their behavior at infinity provide a complementary perspective. El Hilany’s survey [EH25] places the Jacobian problem within the topological classification of polynomial maps, including the study of nonproperness sets and singularities at infinity. In the real planar setting, Braun, Fernandes, Gwoździewicz, and Oréfice-Okamoto [BFGO26] prove injectivity for polynomial maps with nowhere-vanishing Jacobian determinant when one component has degree at most six, and construct a noninjective example with a component of degree seven. Their sharp result concerns real injectivity under a nowhere-vanishing determinant hypothesis. Our use of cubic components and boundary residues addresses polynomial invertibility over ℂ\mathbb{C} under the constant-Jacobian condition.

Formal inverses also enter recent formulations over coefficient rings. Hamada, Kato, and Komiya [HKK25] relate the Jacobian statement for Tate algebras over a ring with Hausdorff adic topology to the polynomial statement over its residue ring, and give a non-Archimedean reformulation over ℂp\mathbb{C}_{p}. Their use of uniqueness of formal inverses offers a related perspective on coefficient descent, which appears below in the extension of invertibility to characteristic-zero fields.

A second question asks how polynomial automorphisms are generated. An automorphism is called tame if it is a composition of affine and elementary automorphisms. Jung [Jun42] and van der Kulk [vdK53] proved that every plane polynomial automorphism is tame. In three variables, Shestakov and Umirbaev [SU04] proved that Nagata’s automorphism is wild, so polynomial invertibility alone does not settle the tameness question. Blanc and van Santen [BvS22] classified automorphisms of affine three-space of total degree at most three up to affine changes of source and target. In particular, every automorphism in that degree range is tame. Their classification also supplies explicit normal forms for the low-degree coordinates that occur below.

In related work [WY26], we study polynomial maps HH in three variables with nilpotent Jacobian over a field KK of characteristic zero. The classification proposed there reduces normalized maps HH, with H⁡(0)=0H(0)=0 and linearly independent components, by constant linear conjugation to the family

𝒩P​(x,y,z)=(P⁡(y+x2),z−2​x​P​(y+x2),P​(y+x2)2),P∈K⁡[t]∖K,P⁡(0)=0.\mathcal{N}_{P}(x,y,z)=\bigl(P(y+x^{2}),\ z-2xP(y+x^{2}),\ P(y+x^{2})^{2}\bigr),\qquad P\in K[t]\setminus K,\quad P(0)=0.

This family has total degree 4​deg⁡P4\deg P, so its first nontrivial members are quartic. The proposed classification leads to explicit inverses and tame factorizations for the one-parameter families id+s​H\mathrm{id}+sH, together with stable-tameness results for specified higher-dimensional block extensions. The methods use algebraically dependent constant linear combinations of the components, generic-fiber geometry, and polynomial derivations. These tools are also relevant here, but the present invertibility proof uses the total degree bound directly and is independent of that classification. In particular, no nilpotence assumption on J⁡(F−id)\operatorname{J}(F-\mathrm{id}) is imposed.

We address invertibility and tameness in total degree at most four. The invertibility argument applies to arbitrary Keller maps of total degree at most four, without an initial automorphism assumption. The tameness argument assumes polynomial invertibility and studies elementary factorizations in the same degree range. Their conclusions combine as follows.

Theorem 1.1.

Let F=(F1,F2,F3)∈ℂ​[x,y,z]3F=(F_{1},F_{2},F_{3})\in\mathbb{C}[x,y,z]^{3} and suppose

max1≤i≤3⁡deg⁡Fi≤4,detJ⁡F∈ℂ∗.\max_{1\leq i\leq 3}\deg F_{i}\leq 4,\qquad\det\operatorname{J}F\in\mathbb{C}^{*}.

Then FF is a tame polynomial automorphism of 𝔸ℂ3\mathbb{A}^{3}_{\mathbb{C}}.

The degree hypothesis is essential to the scope of this statement. Throughout the paper, degree means ordinary total degree. The geometric degree of a dominant generically finite map instead counts the points in a generic fiber. Alpöge’s counterexample has total degree seven, and Gao’s three-dimensional example of geometric degree four has component total degrees (4,11,12)(4,11,12) [Gao26, Theorem 3.5]. Both lie outside the total degree range of Theorem 1.1. The theorem identifies a range in which the Keller condition still forces invertibility and the resulting automorphisms admit tame factorizations.

The proof of invertibility begins with the homogeneous quartic part of FF. Let ρ\rho be the dimension of the span of its three components. When ρ=3\rho=3, homogeneous factorization reduces the leading part to four degree patterns. The binary and common-factor patterns are controlled by successive homogeneous coefficients of the Jacobian determinant. The remaining pattern is a Veronese map composed with a pencil of quadrics. The invariant ring of the associated Jacobian derivation restricts this pencil, and explicit coefficient calculations treat the resulting normal forms. This part of the argument either excludes a leading form or produces a constant second directional derivative.

When ρ≤2\rho\leq 2, a linear target change gives a component RR of degree at most three. On every smooth fiber of RR, the Keller identity makes the residue two-form exact. Periods along the boundary at infinity restrict the cubic leading part of RR, while a second residue calculation excludes the cuspidal case and controls a conic tangent to a line. The remaining components admit coordinate completions with controlled inverse degree, apart from the scalar x+x2​yx+x^{2}y. A formal Laurent-residue argument and a leading-coefficient obstruction exclude that scalar. The coordinate completions reduce invertibility to plane Keller maps of degree at most twenty, well within the established planar bounds [Moh83, GGHV22].

The tameness proof uses the preceding leading-part calculations together with tools specific to automorphisms. We first establish a criterion, without a degree bound, based on a constant second directional derivative. Its affine case uses de Bondt’s classification of quasi-translations [dB18]; its quadratic case uses irreducibility of coordinate fibers. For maps with a component of degree at most three, the classification of Blanc and van Santen [BvS22] reduces the problem to a small number of coordinate forms. Components of the form x+C⁡(y,z)x+C(y,z) lead to families of plane automorphisms over ℂ⁡[t]\mathbb{C}[t]. Furter’s work on fixed multidegrees [Fur09] and the local-to-global theorem of Berson, Dubouloz, Furter, and Maubach [BDFM12] provide the relevant tameness criteria. The remaining cubic form is treated by homogeneous Jacobian identities.

Section 2 fixes the notation and records the algebraic inputs and homogeneous factorization lemma. Section 3 proves invertibility and gives the explicit coefficient certificates used for the conic pencils. Section 4 proves tameness, reusing the leading-part reductions from Section 3. Section 5 discusses the scope of the results and directions for further work.

2. Notation and preliminaries

We collect the notation and algebraic facts used in both proofs. Except in Corollary 3.19, the base field is ℂ\mathbb{C}.

2.1. Polynomial maps and degree conventions

The degree of a polynomial map is its ordinary total degree deg⁡F=maxi⁡deg⁡Fi\deg F=\max_{i}\deg F_{i}. A polynomial map with constant nonzero Jacobian determinant is called a Keller map. A polynomial rr is a coordinate if it is a component of a polynomial automorphism; such an automorphism is called a coordinate completion of rr. An elementary automorphism fixes all but one variable and adds to that variable a polynomial in the others. The group generated by affine and elementary automorphisms is the tame automorphism group. For a coefficient ring RR, the notation GA2⁡(R)\operatorname{GA}_{2}(R) denotes the group of RR-automorphisms of R⁡[u,v]R[u,v]. We regard polynomial maps as column vectors and write J⁡F=(Fx,Fy,Fz)\operatorname{J}F=(F_{x},F_{y},F_{z}) for the Jacobian matrix, whose columns are the partial derivatives of FF.

Independent affine changes of source and target preserve the Keller condition, the total degree bound, and tameness. They need not be simultaneous conjugations. A normalization of the linear part will therefore be used together with a leading normal form only when their compatibility has been justified. The term quartic will refer to the degree range at most four. For a nonzero constant vector ee, ∂e\partial_{e} denotes differentiation in the direction ee. All linear independence statements about polynomial components are over ℂ\mathbb{C} unless another field is specified.

2.2. Homogeneous Jacobian identities

After subtracting the constant term, write

F=H4+H3+H2+H1,Ji=J⁡Hi,F=H_{4}+H_{3}+H_{2}+H_{1},\qquad J_{i}=\operatorname{J}H_{i},

where HiH_{i} is homogeneous of degree ii and a missing homogeneous part is zero. We denote the constant Jacobian determinant by κ≠0\kappa\neq 0. The symbol δ\delta used later denotes a coefficient parameter. For three-by-three matrices set

ℳ⁡(A,B)=[t2]​det(A+t​B),𝒯⁡(A,B,C)=[s​t​u]​det(s​A+t​B+u​C).\mathcal{M}(A,B)=[t^{2}]\det(A+tB),\qquad\mathcal{T}(A,B,C)=[stu]\det(sA+tB+uC).

Thus ℳ\mathcal{M} has one row from AA and two rows from BB, and 𝒯\mathcal{T} is the sum of the six row allocations. If Δj\Delta_{j} denotes the homogeneous degree-jj part of detJ⁡F\det\operatorname{J}F, then

Δ9\displaystyle\Delta_{9} =detJ4,\displaystyle=\det J_{4},
Δ8\displaystyle\Delta_{8} =tr⁡(adj⁡J4​J3),\displaystyle=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}J_{4}\,J_{3}),
(2.1) Δ7\displaystyle\Delta_{7} =tr⁡(adj⁡J4​J2)+ℳ⁡(J4,J3),\displaystyle=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}J_{4}\,J_{2})+\mathcal{M}(J_{4},J_{3}),
Δ6\displaystyle\Delta_{6} =tr⁡(adj⁡J4​J1)+𝒯⁡(J4,J3,J2)+detJ3,\displaystyle=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}J_{4}\,J_{1})+\mathcal{T}(J_{4},J_{3},J_{2})+\det J_{3},
Δ5\displaystyle\Delta_{5} =ℳ⁡(J4,J2)+𝒯⁡(J4,J3,J1)+ℳ⁡(J2,J3).\displaystyle=\mathcal{M}(J_{4},J_{2})+\mathcal{T}(J_{4},J_{3},J_{1})+\mathcal{M}(J_{2},J_{3}).

For a Keller map, all the expressions in (2.1) vanish.

2.3. Algebraic facts

The following results will be used throughout the proof.

A Keller map 𝔸ℂ2→𝔸ℂ2\mathbb{A}^{2}_{\mathbb{C}}\to\mathbb{A}^{2}_{\mathbb{C}} of degree at most twenty is a polynomial automorphism. This is a much weaker consequence of Moh’s bound of one hundred [Moh83].

An injective Keller map of complex affine space is a polynomial automorphism [Ax69, BCW82]. Indeed, injectivity implies surjectivity by Ax’s theorem, and a bijective étale morphism in this setting is an isomorphism.

2.4. Closed polynomial generators

We give proofs of the facts about closed polynomials and algebraic dependence needed below. These are standard facts; see [AP07] for background and further characterizations. All subsequent uses of these facts refer to the proofs below.

Write A=ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]A=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] and L=Frac⁡AL=\operatorname{Frac}A. A nonconstant polynomial s∈As\in A is called closed if every element of AA integral over ℂ⁡[s]\mathbb{C}[s] belongs to ℂ⁡[s]\mathbb{C}[s]. A subfield E⊂LE\subset L is relatively algebraically closed in LL if every element of LL algebraic over EE belongs to EE.

For any nonconstant polynomial ss one has

(2.2) ℂ⁡(s)∩ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]=ℂ⁡[s].\mathbb{C}(s)\cap\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]=\mathbb{C}[s].

Indeed, a Bézout identity for coprime univariate polynomials a,ba,b remains a Bézout identity for a⁡(s),b⁡(s)a(s),b(s). If a⁡(s)/b⁡(s)a(s)/b(s) is polynomial, b⁡(s)b(s) is a unit, and therefore bb is constant. The same argument shows that if a⁡(s)/b⁡(s)=f/ga(s)/b(s)=f/g, where a,ba,b are coprime and f,gf,g are polynomials, then b⁡(s)b(s) divides gg.

Lemma 2.1 (Normal subalgebras in one variable).

Let BB be a ℂ\mathbb{C}-subalgebra of ℂ⁡[t]\mathbb{C}[t] that contains a nonconstant polynomial and is integrally closed in its fraction field. Then B=ℂ⁡[u]B=\mathbb{C}[u] for some u∈ℂ⁡[t]u\in\mathbb{C}[t].

Proof.

Put E=Frac⁡BE=\operatorname{Frac}B, and choose a monic u∈Bu\in B of least positive degree mm. Since tt satisfies the monic equation u⁡(T)−u⁡(t)=0u(T)-u(t)=0 over BB, ℂ⁡[t]\mathbb{C}[t] is integral over BB. Consequently E∩ℂ⁡[t]=BE\cap\mathbb{C}[t]=B.

Let M⁡(T)∈E⁡[T]M(T)\in E[T] be the monic minimal polynomial of tt over EE. It divides u⁡(T)−u⁡(t)u(T)-u(t) in ℂ​(t)​[T]\mathbb{C}(t)[T]. Both MM and the monic quotient NN lie in ℂ⁡[t,T]\mathbb{C}[t,T]: their coefficients are integral over ℂ⁡[t]\mathbb{C}[t] and belong to ℂ⁡(t)\mathbb{C}(t), and ℂ⁡[t]\mathbb{C}[t] is integrally closed. In particular, every coefficient of MM lies in E∩ℂ⁡[t]=BE\cap\mathbb{C}[t]=B. Some coefficient of MM is nonconstant in tt, since M⁡(t)=0M(t)=0 and tt is transcendental over ℂ\mathbb{C}. Its degree is at least mm, by the choice of uu. Taking total degrees in the two independent variables t,Tt,T gives

m=degt,T⁡(u⁡(T)−u⁡(t))=degt,T⁡M+degt,T⁡N.m=\deg_{t,T}\bigl(u(T)-u(t)\bigr)=\deg_{t,T}M+\deg_{t,T}N.

Thus degt,T⁡M≥m\deg_{t,T}M\geq m forces NN to be constant, and [ℂ(t):E]=degTM=m[\mathbb{C}(t):E]=\deg_{T}M=m. The equation u⁡(T)−u⁡(t)=0u(T)-u(t)=0 also gives [ℂ(t):ℂ(u)]≤m[\mathbb{C}(t):\mathbb{C}(u)]\leq m. Since ℂ⁡(u)⊂E\mathbb{C}(u)\subset E, the tower law yields E=ℂ⁡(u)E=\mathbb{C}(u). Finally, the one-variable instance of (2.2) gives B=E∩ℂ⁡[t]=ℂ⁡[u]B=E\cap\mathbb{C}[t]=\mathbb{C}[u]. ∎

Proposition 2.2 (Closed generators).

The following statements hold in AA.

  1. (i)

    Every nonconstant r∈Ar\in A has a representation r=h⁡(s)r=h(s), where h∈ℂ⁡[T]h\in\mathbb{C}[T] and s∈As\in A is closed.

  2. (ii)

    A nonconstant s∈As\in A is closed if and only if ℂ⁡(s)\mathbb{C}(s) is relatively algebraically closed in LL.

  3. (iii)

    If p∈Ap\in A is nonconstant and q∈Aq\in A is algebraic over ℂ⁡(p)\mathbb{C}(p), then p=P⁡(s)p=P(s) and q=Q⁡(s)q=Q(s) for a common closed polynomial s∈As\in A and some P,Q∈ℂ⁡[T]P,Q\in\mathbb{C}[T].

Proof.

For (i), let BB be the integral closure of ℂ⁡[r]\mathbb{C}[r] in LL. Every element of BB is integral over AA and hence belongs to AA, since AA is integrally closed. Transitivity of integrality also shows that BB is integrally closed in its fraction field.

Choose an affine line ℓ:𝔸1→𝔸n\ell:\mathbb{A}^{1}\to\mathbb{A}^{n} on which rr is nonconstant. Such a line can be chosen through two points with distinct rr-values. Restriction to ℓ\ell defines a homomorphism B→ℂ⁡[t]B\to\mathbb{C}[t], and we claim that it is injective. Indeed, any nonzero b∈Bb\in B satisfies a monic equation over ℂ⁡[r]\mathbb{C}[r] whose constant term c⁡(r)c(r) is nonzero: remove any common power of the indeterminate from an integral equation for bb. This equation gives c⁡(r)∈b​Bc(r)\in bB. If bb vanished identically on ℓ\ell, then c⁡(r)c(r) would also vanish there, contradicting the nonconstancy of r|ℓr|_{\ell}. Lemma 2.1 applied to the image therefore gives B=ℂ⁡[s]B=\mathbb{C}[s] for some s∈As\in A. In particular r=h⁡(s)r=h(s). If an element of AA is integral over ℂ⁡[s]=B\mathbb{C}[s]=B, it is integral over ℂ⁡[r]\mathbb{C}[r] and thus belongs to BB. Hence ss is closed.

For (ii), suppose first that ss is closed and that v∈Lv\in L is algebraic over ℂ⁡(s)\mathbb{C}(s). Clearing denominators gives an equation

cd​(s)​vd+cd−1​(s)​vd−1+⋯+c0​(s)=0,ci∈ℂ⁡[T],cd≠0.c_{d}(s)v^{d}+c_{d-1}(s)v^{d-1}+\cdots+c_{0}(s)=0,\qquad c_{i}\in\mathbb{C}[T],\quad c_{d}\neq 0.

Multiplication by cd​(s)d−1c_{d}(s)^{d-1} shows that cd​(s)​vc_{d}(s)v is integral over ℂ⁡[s]\mathbb{C}[s]. It belongs to AA because AA is integrally closed, and then to ℂ⁡[s]\mathbb{C}[s] because ss is closed. Thus v∈ℂ⁡(s)v\in\mathbb{C}(s). Conversely, if ℂ⁡(s)\mathbb{C}(s) is relatively algebraically closed in LL, every element of AA integral over ℂ⁡[s]\mathbb{C}[s] belongs to ℂ⁡(s)\mathbb{C}(s), and hence to ℂ⁡[s]\mathbb{C}[s] by (2.2).

For (iii), apply (i) to pp to obtain p=P⁡(s)p=P(s) with ss closed. The polynomial qq is algebraic over ℂ⁡(s)\mathbb{C}(s), so (ii) gives q∈ℂ⁡(s)q\in\mathbb{C}(s). Equation (2.2) then gives q∈ℂ⁡[s]q\in\mathbb{C}[s]. ∎

Lemma 2.3 (Differential criterion and constants).

Let r∈L∖ℂr\in L\setminus\mathbb{C} and v∈Lv\in L. Then vv is algebraic over ℂ⁡(r)\mathbb{C}(r) if and only if

(∂xir)​(∂xjv)−(∂xjr)​(∂xiv)=0(1≤i<j≤n).(\partial_{x_{i}}r)(\partial_{x_{j}}v)-(\partial_{x_{j}}r)(\partial_{x_{i}}v)=0\qquad(1\leq i<j\leq n).

ker(Ds:ℂ(x,y)→ℂ(x,y))=ℂ(s),ker(Ds:ℂ[x,y]→ℂ[x,y])=ℂ[s].\ker\bigl(D_{s}:\mathbb{C}(x,y)\to\mathbb{C}(x,y)\bigr)=\mathbb{C}(s),\qquad\ker\bigl(D_{s}:\mathbb{C}[x,y]\to\mathbb{C}[x,y]\bigr)=\mathbb{C}[s].
Proof.

If vv is algebraic over ℂ⁡(r)\mathbb{C}(r), differentiate its minimal polynomial relation. Characteristic zero makes the derivative of that polynomial with respect to its indeterminate nonzero at vv. Thus ∂xiv=a​∂xir\partial_{x_{i}}v=a\,\partial_{x_{i}}r for all ii, with the same a∈La\in L, and the displayed minors vanish.

Conversely, if r,vr,v are algebraically independent, extend them to a transcendence basis of L/ℂL/\mathbb{C}. The partial derivations with respect to rr and vv on the resulting purely transcendental subfield extend to ℂ\mathbb{C}-derivations δ,ϵ\delta,\epsilon of LL, since the remaining extension is finite and separable. Explicitly, for an algebraic element α\alpha with minimal polynomial PP, the extension is determined by δ(α)=−δ(P)(α)/P′(α)\delta(\alpha)=-\delta(P)(\alpha)/P^{\prime}(\alpha), where δ⁡(P)\delta(P) differentiates the coefficients; the same formula applies to ϵ\epsilon. Hence

δ⁡(r)=1,δ⁡(v)=0,ϵ⁡(r)=0,ϵ⁡(v)=1.\delta(r)=1,\quad\delta(v)=0,\qquad\epsilon(r)=0,\quad\epsilon(v)=1.

Every ℂ\mathbb{C}-derivation η\eta of LL has the form ∑iη(xi)∂xi\sum_{i}\eta(x_{i})\partial_{x_{i}}. Vanishing of all the displayed minors would therefore imply δ⁡(r)​ϵ​(v)−ϵ⁡(r)​δ​(v)=0\delta(r)\epsilon(v)-\epsilon(r)\delta(v)=0, a contradiction. The two kernel identities now follow from Proposition 2.2(ii) and (2.2). ∎

2.5. Homogeneous factorization

The next lemma organizes the possible quartic leading parts when their components are linearly independent.

Lemma 2.4.

Let H=(H1,H2,H3)H=(H_{1},H_{2},H_{3}) consist of linearly independent homogeneous forms of a common positive degree dd, and suppose detJ⁡H=0\det\operatorname{J}H=0. There are coprime homogeneous forms p,qp,q of the same degree m≥1m\geq 1, coprime binary forms Φi\Phi_{i} of a common degree e≥2e\geq 2, and a homogeneous polynomial gg of degree r≥0r\geq 0 such that

(2.3) Hi=g​Φi​(p,q),d=r+e​m.H_{i}=g\Phi_{i}(p,q),\qquad d=r+em.

For d=4d=4 the possibilities for (r,m,e)(r,m,e) are

(2.4) (0,1,4),(1,1,3),(2,1,2),(0,2,2).(0,1,4),\quad(1,1,3),\quad(2,1,2),\quad(0,2,2).
Proof.

Euler’s identity shows that the radial value vector belongs to the column space of J⁡H\operatorname{J}H. The projective differential rank is one less than the affine rank. If the latter were at most one, the projective image would be a point, contrary to independence. Thus rank⁡J⁡H=2\operatorname{rank}\operatorname{J}H=2, and the image of [H1:H2:H3][H_{1}:H_{2}:H_{3}] is a curve. The restriction to a suitable line in the source is nonconstant. It gives a dominant rational map from ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} to the normalization of that curve, which is therefore rational in characteristic zero. Choose a rational parameter on the normalization; its pullback is p/qp/q for coprime homogeneous forms of equal degree mm. The normalization map to ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} is represented by binary forms Φi\Phi_{i} of a common degree ee without common projective zero. Since the image is not a line, e≥2e\geq 2.

The polynomials Φi​(p,q)\Phi_{i}(p,q) are coprime. Indeed, powers of both binary variables belong to the ideal generated by the Φi\Phi_{i}, so a common irreducible divisor of the substituted forms would divide both pp and qq. The rational proportionality factor between HiH_{i} and Φi​(p,q)\Phi_{i}(p,q) is consequently a homogeneous polynomial gg. This proves (2.3); elementary degree comparison gives (2.4). ∎

3. Invertibility of quartic Keller maps

This section proves the invertibility statement underlying Theorem 1.1. The proof separates maps with three independent quartic leading components from those with a component of degree at most three. The former are treated by homogeneous Jacobian identities; the latter by residue obstructions and coordinate completions with controlled inverse degree.

Theorem 3.1.

Let F∈ℂ​[x,y,z]3F\in\mathbb{C}[x,y,z]^{3} satisfy

deg⁡F:=maxi⁡deg⁡Fi≤4,detJ⁡F∈ℂ∗.\deg F:=\max_{i}\deg F_{i}\leq 4,\qquad\det\operatorname{J}F\in\mathbb{C}^{*}.

Then FF is a polynomial automorphism of 𝔸ℂ3\mathbb{A}^{3}_{\mathbb{C}}.

3.1. A constant second directional derivative

We begin with an invertibility criterion that will apply to several leading forms. The affine reduction below is also used to exclude the exceptional scalar component in Section 3.7.

Write {f,g}=fx​gy−fy​gx\{f,g\}=f_{x}g_{y}-f_{y}g_{x}.

Lemma 3.2 (Affine reduction).

Let a,b,p,q,r∈ℂ⁡[x,y]a,b,p,q,r\in\mathbb{C}[x,y] and suppose

Then p,q∈ℂ⁡[r]p,q\in\mathbb{C}[r], and S=p​b−q​aS=pb-qa satisfies {S,r}=κ\{S,r\}=\kappa.

Proof.

The third column of the Jacobian matrix shows that p,qp,q have no common zero. By Proposition 2.2(i), write r=h⁡(s)r=h(s) with ss a closed generator. Since h′​(s)h^{\prime}(s) divides every entry of the third Jacobian row, it divides κ\kappa; thus hh is affine linear and rr is itself closed. Interchange the first two components if needed so that q≠0q\neq 0. The coefficient of zz is p⁡{q,r}−q⁡{p,r}=0p\{q,r\}-q\{p,r\}=0, so {p/q,r}=0\{p/q,r\}=0. Since rr is closed, the rational-function kernel identity in Lemma 2.3 gives p/q∈ℂ⁡(r)p/q\in\mathbb{C}(r). Write p/q=A⁡(r)/B⁡(r)p/q=A(r)/B(r) in reduced form. Bézout gives p=η​A​(r)p=\eta A(r), q=η​B​(r)q=\eta B(r) for a polynomial η\eta; the absence of a common zero makes η\eta constant. {p​b−q​a,r}=p⁡{b,r}−q⁡{a,r}=κ.\{pb-qa,r\}=p\{b,r\}-q\{a,r\}=\kappa.

∎

3.3. Coprime conic pencils without a square

The remaining pattern in (2.4) factors through a pencil of quadrics. Write 𝝂⁡(s,t)=(s2,s​t,t2)T\boldsymbol{\nu}(s,t)=(s^{2},st,t^{2})^{T}. We first determine the polynomial first integrals of the pencil derivation, using homogeneous degrees on its generic conic.

Lemma 3.7 (Smooth generic member).

Let p,q∈ℂ⁡[x,y,z]p,q\in\mathbb{C}[x,y,z] be coprime homogeneous quadrics whose pencil contains no square of a nonzero linear form. Then p,qp,q are algebraically independent, and the generic projective member of their pencil is a smooth conic.

Proof.

The quadrics are linearly independent by coprimeness. Two homogeneous forms of the same degree that are algebraically dependent are proportional: decompose a polynomial relation by degree, and use the factorization of the resulting homogeneous binary relation over ℂ\mathbb{C}. Thus p,qp,q are algebraically independent.

Suppose every member of the pencil were singular. No nonzero member has rank one, since over ℂ\mathbb{C} such a quadratic form is a square up to a nonzero scalar. Choose a rank-two member as q=x​yq=xy and write

p=a​x2+b​x​y+c​y2+d​x​z+e​y​z+f​z2.p=ax^{2}+bxy+cy^{2}+dxz+eyz+fz^{2}.

The determinant of the symmetric matrix of p+t​x​yp+txy is

a​c​f+(b+t)​d​e4−a​e2+c​d24−f​(b+t)24.acf+\frac{(b+t)de}{4}-\frac{ae^{2}+cd^{2}}{4}-\frac{f(b+t)^{2}}{4}.

Its identically vanishing coefficients give f=0f=0, d​e=0de=0, and a​e2+c​d2=0ae^{2}+cd^{2}=0. If d≠0d\neq 0, then e=c=0e=c=0, so xx divides both p,qp,q. If e≠0e\neq 0, then d=a=0d=a=0, so yy divides both. If d=e=0d=e=0, both quadrics are binary. The homogeneous quadratic determinant of a binary pencil either vanishes identically or has a projective zero over ℂ\mathbb{C}. In either event, some nonzero binary member has rank one, hence is a square. All cases contradict the hypotheses. The ternary pencil determinant is therefore nonzero, which proves the assertion also at its generic parameter. ∎

Lemma 3.8.

Let p,q∈ℂ⁡[x,y,z]p,q\in\mathbb{C}[x,y,z] be coprime homogeneous quadrics. If their pencil contains no square of a nonzero linear form, then

kerℂ⁡[x,y,z]𝒟=ℂ[p,q],𝒟=(∇p×∇q)⋅∇.\operatorname{ker}_{\mathbb{C}[x,y,z]}\mathcal{D}=\mathbb{C}[p,q],\qquad\mathcal{D}=(\nabla p\times\nabla q)\cdot\nabla.
Proof.

The inclusion ℂ⁡[p,q]⊆ker⁡𝒟\mathbb{C}[p,q]\subseteq\operatorname{ker}\mathcal{D} follows from the definition of 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Since 𝒟\mathcal{D} raises degree by one, it suffices to treat a nonzero homogeneous invariant ff of degree d>0d>0.

Put K=ℂ⁡(λ)K=\mathbb{C}(\lambda), with λ\lambda indeterminate. Lemma 3.7 shows that

C={p−λq=0}⊂ℙK2C=\{p-\lambda q=0\}\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}_{K}

is a smooth conic. The two projective conics p=0p=0 and q=0q=0 have a common point over ℂ\mathbb{C} by Bézout. This is a KK-rational point of CC, and projection from it gives K⁡(C)≃K⁡(t)K(C)\simeq K(t). Thus a rational function on CC with zero differential belongs to KK.

Restriction to the affine cone over CC does not annihilate a nonzero polynomial with complex coefficients: clear denominators in λ\lambda and substitute λ=p/q\lambda=p/q. At its generic point, ∇p,∇q\nabla p,\nabla q are independent, and 𝒟​f=0\mathcal{D}f=0 gives ∇f=u∇p+v∇q\nabla f=u\nabla p+v\nabla q. Euler’s identity yields 2​q​(λ​u+v)=d​f2q(\lambda u+v)=d\,f. On a projective chart of CC we have d​p=λ​d​q\mathrm{d}p=\lambda\mathrm{d}q, hence

(3.10) q​d​f=d2​f​d​q,d⁡(f2qd)=0.q\,\mathrm{d}f=\frac{d}{2}f\,\mathrm{d}q,\qquad\mathrm{d}\left(\frac{f^{2}}{q^{d}}\right)=0.

The degree-zero ratio f2/qdf^{2}/q^{d} is therefore in KK. Substituting λ=p/q\lambda=p/q gives

f2=qd​c​(p/q),c∈ℂ⁡(λ).f^{2}=q^{d}c(p/q),\qquad c\in\mathbb{C}(\lambda).

The denominator factors qq and p−a​qp-aq for distinct a∈ℂa\in\mathbb{C} are pairwise coprime. Polynomiality of f2f^{2} consequently forbids finite poles of cc and forces deg⁡c≤d\deg c\leq d. Thus

f2=H⁡(p,q),H∈ℂ⁡[s,t]​ homogeneous of degree ​d.f^{2}=H(p,q),\qquad H\in\mathbb{C}[s,t]\text{ homogeneous of degree }d.

Distinct binary linear factors of HH give coprime pencil members. Each member is squarefree, since a non-squarefree quadratic over ℂ\mathbb{C} is a scalar multiple of a square. Unique factorization in ℂ⁡[x,y,z]\mathbb{C}[x,y,z] therefore forces every linear factor of HH to have even multiplicity. If a quartic Keller map has H4=𝛎⁡(p,q)H_{4}=\boldsymbol{\nu}(p,q) for coprime homogeneous quadrics p,qp,q, then the pencil ⟨p,q⟩\langle p,q\rangle contains a square.

3.4. The two nonbinary square pencils

Proposition 3.9 reduces the conic-pencil analysis to pencils containing a square. We classify these pencils and then use the degree-seven and degree-six Jacobian equations to exclude the nonbinary normal forms. If the pencil contains a square, choose it as p=x2p=x^{2}. Classify the rank of qq on the plane x=0x=0. Rank two gives q=y​zq=yz after a linear change of y,zy,z, further linear changes to remove the cross terms involving xx, and subtraction of a multiple of x2x^{2}. Rank one gives q=y2q=y^{2} or q=y2+x​zq=y^{2}+xz. Rank zero would make qq divisible by xx, contradicting coprimeness. Pencil changes induce invertible constant changes of the three Veronese components. Hence the possibilities are

(3.12) (p,q)=(x2,y2),(x2,y​z),(x2,y2+x​z).(p,q)=(x^{2},y^{2}),\qquad(x^{2},yz),\qquad(x^{2},y^{2}+xz).

The first is covered by Lemma 3.5.

Proposition 3.10.

If H4=𝛎⁡(p,q)H_{4}=\boldsymbol{\nu}(p,q) for coprime homogeneous quadrics, a quartic Keller map is an automorphism. More precisely, a nonsquare pencil and both nonbinary square-pencil normal forms have no quartic Keller completion; the remaining binary form satisfies Proposition 3.3.

Proof.

Combine Proposition 3.9, (3.12), the two exclusions above, and Lemma 3.5. ∎

Proposition 3.11.

If the three components of H4H_{4} are linearly independent, a quartic Keller map FF is a polynomial automorphism.

Proof.

Apply Lemma 2.4. For (r,m,e)=(0,1,4)(r,m,e)=(0,1,4) the leading part is binary, so Lemma 3.5 applies. For (1,1,3)(1,1,3), take p=x,q=yp=x,q=y. The linear common factor gg is either binary, or it can be taken as the third source coordinate. Both cases are covered by Lemma 3.5.

For (2,1,2)(2,1,2), the three independent binary quadrics are a basis of the binary quadratic space, so a target change gives H4=g⁡(x2,x​y,y2)H_{4}=g(x^{2},xy,y^{2}). If gg is independent of zz, use Lemma 3.5. If g=g1​(x,y)​z+g2​(x,y)g=g_{1}(x,y)z+g_{2}(x,y) has zz-degree one, its zz coefficient g1​(x,y)​(x2,x​y,y2)g_{1}(x,y)(x^{2},xy,y^{2}) has independent components, so use Lemma 3.5. If its zz-degree is two, Lemma 3.6 excludes this case.

The remaining pattern (0,2,2)(0,2,2) is exactly Proposition 3.10. These exhaust (2.4). ∎

3.5. A component of degree at most three: residue and boundary

We now treat F=(P,Q,R)F=(P,Q,R) with

(3.27) deg⁡P,deg⁡Q≤4,deg⁡R≤3,detJ⁡(P,Q,R)=κ≠0.\deg P,\deg Q\leq 4,\qquad\deg R\leq 3,\qquad\det\operatorname{J}(P,Q,R)=\kappa\neq 0.

The component RR has no critical point. We first record how a coordinate completion with bounded inverse degree reduces the problem to planar invertibility.

Lemma 3.12.

Suppose, after affine source changes and affine rescaling of RR, that RR is a component of a polynomial automorphism Θ\Theta with deg⁡Θ−1≤5\deg\Theta^{-1}\leq 5. Then every map satisfying (3.27) is a polynomial automorphism.

Proof.

Compose with Θ−1\Theta^{-1} and permute the target coordinates to make the third component an affine coordinate. The new total degree is at most 4⋅5=204\cdot 5=20. On each fiber of the third source coordinate, the first two components form a planar Keller map of degree at most twenty, with a nonzero constant determinant. Every such map is injective by the planar invertibility theorem. Equality of the three target coordinates therefore forces equality in the source. The injectivity criterion then gives polynomial invertibility. ∎

If deg⁡R≤2\deg R\leq 2, Lemma 3.12 already applies with inverse degree at most two. To justify the only nontrivial case, write the quadratic part as a symmetric form. If the linear part vanished on its radical, it would be in the image of the corresponding symmetric linear map and the gradient would vanish somewhere. Thus the linear part is nonzero on the radical. A linear change in that radical puts RR in the form z+q⁡(x,y)z+q(x,y), up to an affine constant, where deg⁡q≤2\deg q\leq 2. Henceforth assume deg⁡R=3\deg R=3.

3.5.1. The exact fiber form

For each t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C} the affine surface St={R=t}S_{t}=\{R=t\} is smooth. Its residue two-form αt\alpha_{t} is specified by

d​R∧αt=d​x∧d​y∧d​z,\mathrm{d}R\wedge\alpha_{t}=\mathrm{d}x\wedge\mathrm{d}y\wedge\mathrm{d}z,

interpreted locally and then restricted to StS_{t}. On Rz≠0R_{z}\neq 0 it is d​x∧d​y/Rz\mathrm{d}x\wedge\mathrm{d}y/R_{z}; these expressions glue. The Keller identity gives

(3.28) d⁡(P|St)∧d⁡(Q|St)=κ​αt,αt=d⁡(κ−1​P​d​Q)|St.\mathrm{d}(P|_{S_{t}})\wedge\mathrm{d}(Q|_{S_{t}})=\kappa\alpha_{t},\qquad\alpha_{t}=\mathrm{d}\bigl(\kappa^{-1}P\mathrm{d}Q\bigr)|_{S_{t}}.

Thus the residue form is the exterior derivative of the displayed regular algebraic one-form, with the normalization fixed by κ\kappa.

3.5.2. Boundary periods

Lemma 3.13.

Under (3.27) with deg⁡R=3\deg R=3, the plane cubic C={R3=0}⊂ℙ2C=\{R_{3}=0\}\subset\mathbb{P}^{2} is not reduced nodal. Smooth plane cubics are included in the excluded class.

Proof.

Suppose CC is reduced nodal. Fix t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C} and let Xt⊂ℙ3X_{t}\subset\mathbb{P}^{3} be the projective closure of StS_{t}, with boundary C=Xt∩{w=0}C=X_{t}\cap\{w=0\}. The surface XtX_{t} is smooth along CsmC^{\mathrm{sm}}: a derivative of R3R_{3} tangent to the plane at infinity is nonzero there.

The form αt\alpha_{t} has a simple pole along CsmC^{\mathrm{sm}}, with a nowhere-vanishing holomorphic residue one-form η\eta. At smooth boundary points these expressions, with u,vu,v exchanged when necessary, define the asserted global residue η\eta.

Exactness of αt\alpha_{t} forces every period of η\eta on CsmC^{\mathrm{sm}} to vanish. Indeed, over a closed loop γ⊂Csm\gamma\subset C^{\mathrm{sm}} take the oriented normal-circle tube Tρ​(γ)⊂StT_{\rho}(\gamma)\subset S_{t} of small radius ρ\rho. In local coordinates (s,w)(s,w) on XtX_{t}, the form is (d​w/w)∧(a⁡(s,w)​d​s)(\mathrm{d}w/w)\wedge(a(s,w)\mathrm{d}s) and η=a⁡(s,0)​d​s\eta=a(s,0)\mathrm{d}s. If CC has a node, choose analytic plane coordinates at that node and multiply the local defining equation by a unit so that f⁡(u,v,0)=u​vf(u,v,0)=uv. The numerator in (3.29) remains a unit. On the punctured branch v=0v=0,

η=e⁡(u,0,0)​d​uu,∫|u|=εη=2​π​i​e​(0)≠0,\eta=e(u,0,0)\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{u},\qquad\int_{|u|=\varepsilon}\eta=2\pi i\,e(0)\neq 0,

A reduced irreducible plane cubic is smooth, nodal, or cuspidal. A reduced conic and line intersect transversely or are tangent. Three distinct lines are either nonconcurrent, giving nodes, or concurrent. A nonreduced cubic is a double line plus a line or a triple line. Consequently Lemma 3.13 leaves, after linear source changes and rescaling,

(3.31) R3∈ℂ⁡[x,y],R3=x2​y+z3,R3=x2​y+x​z2.R_{3}\in\mathbb{C}[x,y],\qquad R_{3}=x^{2}y+z^{3},\qquad R_{3}=x^{2}y+xz^{2}.

The first alternative includes all repeated-line and concurrent-line configurations.

3.5.3. A common residue obstruction

The regular algebraic primitive in (3.28) also gives the following obstruction for components of a specific form.

Lemma 3.14.

Let R=x2​y+p0​(z)+x​p1​(z)R=x^{2}y+p_{0}(z)+xp_{1}(z), with d=deg⁡p0≥2d=\deg p_{0}\geq 2 and deg⁡p1≤d\deg p_{1}\leq d. αt=−d​x∧d​zx2=d⁡(d​zx).\alpha_{t}=-\frac{\mathrm{d}x\wedge\mathrm{d}z}{x^{2}}=\mathrm{d}\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{x}\right).

3.6.3. A planar submersion lemma

Lemma 3.15.

A polynomial r∈ℂ⁡[x,y]r\in\mathbb{C}[x,y] of degree at most three with no critical point is, up to affine source changes and affine rescaling, either of the form A​y+h⁡(x)Ay+h(x) with A≠0A\neq 0, or x+x2​yx+x^{2}y.

3.8. Proof of invertibility

The independent-leading-part case was settled in Proposition 3.11. We combine the remaining scalar reductions and then complete the proof of Theorem 3.1.

Proposition 3.18.

A map satisfying (3.27) is a polynomial automorphism.

Proof.

Proposition 3.16 gives either a coordinate completion of inverse degree at most five or the exceptional scalar, after affine changes. In the first case apply Lemma 3.12; in the second apply Proposition 3.17. Affine changes preserve the total degree bounds. ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.1.

Subtract the constant term of FF and let H4H_{4} be its quartic homogeneous part. If the three components of H4H_{4} are linearly independent, Proposition 3.11 applies. Otherwise there is a nonzero constant linear form on the target annihilating H4H_{4}. Complete it to an invertible constant target transformation and write the resulting map as (P,Q,R)(P,Q,R) with deg⁡R≤3\deg R\leq 3. The component RR cannot be constant because the Jacobian is nonzero. The other two degrees are still at most four. Proposition 3.18 applies. This includes H4=0H_{4}=0 and therefore degrees smaller than four. Reversing the affine transformations proves the assertion. ∎

Corollary 3.19.

The conclusion of Theorem 3.1 holds over every characteristic-zero field.

Proof.

The coefficients of the map lie in a finitely generated extension K0K_{0} of ℚ\mathbb{Q}, which embeds in ℂ\mathbb{C}. The complex result gives a polynomial inverse after that embedding. Translate and normalize at the origin over K0K_{0}. The formal inverse has coefficients in K0K_{0}, by recursive inversion of its invertible linear part. Uniqueness identifies it with the complex polynomial inverse, so it has finite support and belongs to K0​[𝑿]3K_{0}[\boldsymbol{X}]^{3}. The two inverse identities then hold over K0K_{0} and after any extension of scalars. ∎

4. Tameness of quartic automorphisms

We now prove tameness under an independent automorphism assumption. The argument combines a directional criterion with the classification of low-degree coordinates and local tameness of plane polynomial families. The leading-part calculations in Section 3 will also be used, without repeating their coefficient computations.

Theorem 4.1 (Tameness).

Every complex polynomial automorphism of 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3} of total degree at most four is tame.

4.1. The directional criterion for tameness

We first strengthen the directional invertibility criterion of Proposition 3.3 under the assumption that the map is an automorphism. The resulting tameness criterion requires no degree bound.

Proposition 4.2.

Let F∈Autℂ⁡(𝔸3)F\in\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{C}}(\mathbb{A}^{3}), with no degree assumption. If ∂e2F\partial_{e}^{2}F is constant for some nonzero constant vector ee, then FF is tame.

Proof.

After a linear source change, take ∂e=∂z\partial_{e}=\partial_{z} and write

F=A⁡(x,y)+z​B​(x,y)+z2​E,E∈ℂ3.F=A(x,y)+zB(x,y)+z^{2}E,\qquad E\in\mathbb{C}^{3}.

Every nonzero linear combination ℓ⁡(F)\ell(F) of the components is a coordinate, so ℓ⁡(F)−d\ell(F)-d is irreducible for each d∈ℂd\in\mathbb{C}.

4.2. Small coordinate components and polynomial families

Suppose the quartic leading components span a space of dimension at most two. A linear target change then produces a component of degree at most three. We combine the low-degree coordinate classification with local tameness over ℂ⁡[t]\mathbb{C}[t], beginning with an exclusion needed in both parts of the argument.

4.2.1. An elementary exclusion of the Nagata component

Lemma 4.3.

The coordinate rd=z+x⁡(x​y+z2+d)r_{d}=z+x(xy+z^{2}+d) cannot be completed to an automorphism (P,Q,rd)(P,Q,r_{d}) with deg⁡P,deg⁡Q≤4\deg P,\deg Q\leq 4.

Set s=x​y+z2+ds=xy+z^{2}+d, q=y−2​z​s−x​s2q=y-2zs-xs^{2}, and r=z+x​sr=z+xs. The automorphism (x,q,r)(x,q,r) preserves ss, and s=x​q+r2+ds=xq+r^{2}+d. Work on the generic fiber r=cr=c over K=ℂ⁡(c)K=\mathbb{C}(c), and put D=c2+dD=c^{2}+d. Its inverse coordinates are

(4.2) z=c−x⁡(x​q+D),y=q+2​c​(x​q+D)−x​(x​q+D)2.z=c-x(xq+D),\qquad y=q+2c(xq+D)-x(xq+D)^{2}.

We use the following consequence of the Jung–van der Kulk theorem: over an algebraically closed field, the highest homogeneous part of a plane coordinate is a nonzero scalar multiple of a power of a linear form. Indeed, in a reduced affine–triangular decomposition, each nonlinear degree-increasing step replaces the highest form of one component by a scalar multiple of a power of the other. Starting with an affine pair gives the assertion; a final affine combination either retains that highest form or recovers the preceding component. Apply this observation after extending scalars from KK to K¯\overline{K}, which preserves both the coordinate property and degree. If the highest form of a restricted coordinate of degree mm is λ​(α​x+β​q)m\lambda(\alpha x+\beta q)^{m}, then α,β\alpha,\beta are not both zero. Its degree is therefore attained on the xx-axis or the qq-axis. The bounds on the two axis restrictions consequently give

(4.3) deg⁡P¯,deg⁡Q¯≤4.\deg\bar{P},\deg\bar{Q}\leq 4.

Use the Laurent curve

(x,y,z)=(−t,D/t,t−1−c),r=c,q=−t−3+2​c​t−2+D​t−1.(x,y,z)=(-t,D/t,t^{-1}-c),\qquad r=c,\qquad q=-t^{-3}+2ct^{-2}+Dt^{-1}.

Let uu be either restricted coordinate and m=deg⁡u≤4m=\deg u\leq 4. If m≥2m\geq 2, the monomial qmq^{m} has the unique greatest pole order 3​m>43m>4, so its coefficient vanishes. The pure-power leading form of uu must therefore be a multiple of xmx^{m}. The remaining terms have degree at most three, where the pole orders 3​j−i3j-i are pairwise distinct; any term with j≥2j\geq 2 has pole order at least five and hence vanishes. Thus, also when m=1m=1, we have u=A⁡(x)​q+h⁡(x)u=A(x)q+h(x) over KK. If AA is nonconstant, choose a root aa over K¯\overline{K}. A⁡(r)​q+h⁡(x,r),A∈ℂ⁡[r],h∈ℂ⁡[x,r].A(r)q+h(x,r),\qquad A\in\mathbb{C}[r],\quad h\in\mathbb{C}[x,r].

4.2.2. The cases ρ≤1\rho\leq 1

The cases with at most one independent quartic leading component follow from the degree-three classification and the preceding exclusion. If ρ=0\rho=0, tameness follows from [BvS22, Corollary 3.9.5]. If ρ=1\rho=1, choose two components of degree at most three. The inverse image of each affine line under this pair is 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}. The characteristic-zero cases (4)–(7) of [BvS22, Theorem 3] apply. The first three have tame completions; the last contains the coordinate of Lemma 4.3 and is excluded. For the first three, the completions are triangular or are obtained from

(x+y​z+z​a​(x,z),y+a⁡(x,z)+r⁡(z),z)(x+yz+za(x,z),\ y+a(x,z)+r(z),\ z)

by projection. The displayed automorphism is a composition of three shears. Any other completion of the same pair differs by an affine automorphism of the remaining variable over the polynomial ring in that pair, and is also tame.

4.2.3. Plane automorphisms over ℂ⁡[t]\mathbb{C}[t]

For the remaining coordinate forms, we will use the following local criteria and their passage to global tameness.

Lemma 4.4.

Let Φ∈GA2⁡(ℂ⁡[t])\Phi\in\operatorname{GA}_{2}(\mathbb{C}[t]).

  1. (i)

    At a fiber where the maximum plane degree equals the generic degree, Φ\Phi is tame over the corresponding local ring.

  2. (ii)

    Over a DVR, every plane automorphism of generic degree at most three is tame.

  3. (iii)

    If Φ\Phi is tame at every closed point of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}, it is tame over ℂ⁡[t]\mathbb{C}[t].

Proof.

For (i), let R=ℂ​[t](t−c)R=\mathbb{C}[t]_{(t-c)}, let K=ℂ⁡(t)K=\mathbb{C}(t), and write a bar for specialization at t=ct=c. A polynomial over RR is called primitive if at least one coefficient is a unit. Thus the highest homogeneous part of a component is primitive precisely when its degree is preserved by specialization. Any finite sequence of transformations over RR is defined on a sufficiently small connected open neighborhood of cc.

Here multidegree denotes the ordered sequence of degrees of the nonlinear triangular factors in a reduced Jung–van der Kulk decomposition, rather than the pair of component degrees (deg⁡p,deg⁡q)(\deg p,\deg q). We first recall two consequences of this normal form over a field. For an automorphism with unequal component degrees 1<d<D1<d<D, one has D=j​dD=jd with j≥2j\geq 2, and the higher-degree component can be reduced to degree less than dd by subtracting a polynomial in the lower-degree component. Moreover, the degree of this last triangular factor is j=D/dj=D/d; it is the entry of the multidegree removed first by this degree reduction. Consequently, for two unequal-degree pairs with the same multidegree and the same maximum degree DD, the smaller degree is the same. These assertions follow by reading the final triangular factor of a reduced decomposition.

Write Φ=(p,q)\Phi=(p,q) and induct on deg⁡p+deg⁡q\deg p+\deg q, maintaining the hypothesis that the generic and special maximum degrees agree. If either component is linear, the straightening argument in (ii) below already proves tameness. We may therefore assume that both generic component degrees exceed one. After shrinking around cc, the degree is constant on a connected open neighborhood. By [Fur09, Corollary 3], the multidegree is therefore constant in this family, so the generic and special fibers have the same multidegree. If both generic degrees equal D>1D>1, choose the component whose highest form is primitive and call it qq; such a component exists because the special maximum degree is DD. Over KK, the highest forms satisfy pD=λ​qDp_{D}=\lambda q_{D}. A unit coefficient of qDq_{D} shows that λ∈R\lambda\in R. The elementary change (p,q)↦(p−λ​q,q)(p,q)\mapsto(p-\lambda q,q) reduces the sum of the generic degrees, while qq retains degree DD in both fibers. The induction hypothesis applies to this new pair.

It remains to consider unequal generic degrees d=deg⁡q<D=deg⁡pd=\deg q<D=\deg p. The specialization of pp has degree DD, and that of qq has degree at most d<Dd<D. It cannot become linear: the special multidegree would then have the single entry DD, whereas d>1d>1 gives at least two entries in the generic multidegree. Constancy of multidegree and the preceding normal-form observation therefore force deg⁡q¯=d\deg\bar{q}=d. Hence qdq_{d} is primitive. Over KK, subtract the polynomial in qq that reduces pp below degree dd. Each coefficient in this polynomial belongs to RR: at a step with current degree j​d≥djd\geq d, the highest-form identity is pj​d=λ​qdjp_{jd}=\lambda q_{d}^{j}. Since qdq_{d} is primitive, its reduction is nonzero, and so is the reduction of qdjq_{d}^{j}. Thus qdjq_{d}^{j} has a unit coefficient, and λ∈R\lambda\in R. Subtracting λ​qj\lambda q^{j} preserves integrality of all coefficients. Repeating, including a linear term when needed, gives p′=p−A⁡(q)p^{\prime}=p-A(q) with A∈R⁡[T]A\in R[T] and deg⁡p′<d\deg p^{\prime}<d. The pair (p′,q)(p^{\prime},q) has generic and special maximum degree dd, since qdq_{d} remains primitive. Its degree sum is smaller, so induction applies. The process terminates at an affine automorphism over RR. This proves (i).

For (ii), let RR be a DVR with fraction field KK. If a component is linear, one of its linear coefficients is a unit: otherwise its specialization would be constant, contrary to invertibility of the specialized map. An affine change over RR therefore makes this component a source variable. Over KK, the other component is then linear in the remaining variable; its coefficients lie in RR and its linear coefficient is a unit, since the Jacobian determinant is a unit. Thus the resulting automorphism is triangular over RR. If neither component is linear, their degrees are (2,2)(2,2) or (3,3)(3,3); the pair (2,3)(2,3) is excluded by the plane degree-divisibility theorem. Their highest forms are proportional over KK. For the proportionality coefficient, either it or its reciprocal lies in RR, so an elementary linear change over RR lowers one component degree. The resulting unequal degrees force a linear component, again by divisibility. This reduces to the preceding case.

Finally, (iii) follows from [BDFM12, Theorem 3], since every invertible module over ℂ⁡[t]\mathbb{C}[t] is free. The generic localization is a field and hence is tame by the Jung–van der Kulk theorem, so checking the closed points suffices. ∎

Assume ρ=2\rho=2 and take F=(P,Q,R)F=(P,Q,R) with deg⁡R≤3\deg R\leq 3. A quadratic coordinate has no critical point. Its linear part is nonzero on the radical of its quadratic part, so affine changes put it in one of the forms

4.4. Proof of tameness

We first apply the leading-part calculations from Section 3 to automorphisms. The cases with dependent quartic leading components have been treated above.

Proposition 4.6.

Let F∈Autℂ⁡(𝔸3)F\in\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{C}}(\mathbb{A}^{3}) have total degree at most four, and suppose that the homogeneous quartic components of FF are linearly independent. Then FF is tame.

Proof.

The homogeneous factorization of Lemma 2.4 gives the four patterns (2.4). In the two binary patterns, the proof of Lemma 3.5 produces a constant second derivative in the zz direction. For the quadratic common-factor pattern, either the same lemma applies or Lemma 3.6 contradicts the Jacobian condition. The remaining pattern is a conic pencil: in the absence of a square, Proposition 3.9 excludes it; with a square, Proposition 3.10 excludes the two nonbinary normal forms and reduces the binary normal form to Lemma 3.5. In every remaining case, the map therefore has a constant second directional derivative. Proposition 4.2 then proves tameness. ∎

Proof of Theorem 4.1.

Let ρ\rho denote the dimension of the span of the homogeneous quartic components. If ρ=3\rho=3, apply Proposition 4.6. If ρ=0\rho=0, use the degree-three theorem of Blanc–van Santen [BvS22, Corollary 3.9.5]. For ρ=1\rho=1, the two lower-degree components are treated in Section 4.2.2; the only exceptional cubic-coordinate case is excluded by Lemma 4.3. Finally, for ρ=2\rho=2, choose a target component RR of degree at most three. If it is of the form x+C⁡(y,z)x+C(y,z), Section 4.2 treats it by local tameness and polynomial reduction. The remaining cubic normal form is handled in Section 4.3. These cases exhaust the possibilities. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Theorem 3.1 gives polynomial invertibility, and Theorem 4.1 gives tameness. ∎

5. Concluding remarks

The two proofs address complementary aspects of polynomial maps in the quartic degree range. The invertibility argument reduces the Keller condition to homogeneous leading-part constraints and geometric obstructions on cubic fibers. The tameness argument then combines those constraints with coordinate classifications and local elementary factorizations. The constant second directional derivative provides a common criterion linking the two arguments.

The distinction between invertibility and tameness also affects the scope of the field statements.

Remark 5.1 (Scope of the field statement).

The descent of polynomial invertibility in Corollary 3.19 uses uniqueness of the formal inverse. It does not, by itself, descend a tame factorization from ℂ\mathbb{C} to an arbitrary characteristic-zero field. Accordingly, Theorem 1.1 is formulated over ℂ\mathbb{C}.

Two open questions provide natural directions for future study:

  1. (1)

    Degree five. Is every polynomial map F:𝔸ℂ3→𝔸ℂ3F:\mathbb{A}^{3}_{\mathbb{C}}\to\mathbb{A}^{3}_{\mathbb{C}} of ordinary total degree five satisfying detJ⁡F∈ℂ∗\det\operatorname{J}F\in\mathbb{C}^{*} a polynomial automorphism? If so, is it tame?

  2. (2)

    Degree six. Is every polynomial map F:𝔸ℂ3→𝔸ℂ3F:\mathbb{A}^{3}_{\mathbb{C}}\to\mathbb{A}^{3}_{\mathbb{C}} of ordinary total degree six satisfying detJ⁡F∈ℂ∗\det\operatorname{J}F\in\mathbb{C}^{*} a polynomial automorphism? If so, is it tame?

Further directions include extracting explicit tame factorizations from the reductions in Section 4, with quantitative bounds on the number and degrees of the elementary factors. It is also natural to determine which parts of the leading-form and residue arguments extend beyond the quartic degree range. Such extensions would require a corresponding analysis of the additional leading-part patterns and higher-degree coordinate components. The present proof also suggests studying descent of tame factorizations separately from descent of polynomial inverses.
